A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Search Arena study and provide readable text, figures, tables, mathematical notation, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the conference reformatting and renumbering; v2 adds Appendix G.

before.justification: V1 reports original analyses of 24,069 conversations and 12,652 preference votes, including model rankings, citation analyses, cross-arena experiments, and offline benchmark evaluations.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds expert–user agreement measurements, a reasoning-model citation-source comparison, and analyses of CORAL and WildChat.

M1.justification: The pairwise collection platform, nine-category intent taxonomy, annotation and citation-attribution pipelines, and Bradley–Terry framework remain unchanged. The additions are validation and comparative analyses rather than changes to the proposed procedures.

E1.justification: New Appendix G analyzes CORAL conversational-RAG data and WildChat general-chat logs, extending the dataset-distribution comparisons. The Search Arena collection and existing model-evaluation tasks remain unchanged; neither added dataset becomes a model-performance benchmark here.

E2.justification: The corresponding model tables and performance comparisons retain the same Perplexity, Gemini, and OpenAI variants. Figure E.3 compares two already evaluated models. CORAL and WildChat are dataset comparisons, while the newly cited WildBench is not evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a vote-validation study using 100 samples and three expert annotators, excluding ties when measuring agreement. Appendix G specifies a random 100,000-example sample from filtered WildChat. Existing cross-arena and offline benchmark protocols are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds focused supplementary checks: expert validation of user votes, citation-source distributions for sonar-pro-high versus sonar-reasoning-pro-high using the same search module, and CORAL/WildChat conversation-length and prompt-length comparisons. Existing subgroup analyses and feature controls remain.

E5.justification: Existing bootstrap estimates, confidence intervals, p-values, and benchmark uncertainty ranges are retained. The added expert–user agreement is a point estimate without a reported interval or significance test; no new run counts, seeds, or distinct uncertainty-estimation procedure are introduced.

E6.justification: Existing leaderboard and cross-benchmark scores are unchanged in Tables A3/A4 versus D.1/F.1. New results include 68% expert–user agreement, more community/blog and fewer Wikipedia citations from the reasoning variant, and mean prompt lengths of 12.1 words for CORAL and 594.9 for WildChat.

T1.justification: The claim–citation definitions and mathematical analysis remain unchanged. Neither version contains new theoretical propositions or proofs relative to the other; the added RAG positioning and causal qualifications are conceptual discussion.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims about the preference dataset, citation-related preference patterns, and cross-arena performance. New validation and dataset comparisons support these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: Section 3 newly distinguishes subjective, intent-dependent preferences from objective correctness and explicitly characterizes the analysis as correlational. Section 5 adds specific limitations concerning objective quality metrics, online-evaluation scalability, and when search should be used. Core interpretations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds legacy-interface provenance and dataset-removal contact and privacy-policy information. Section 3.2 explicitly states 800 citation-analysis samples, while Appendix E.3 retains 780 successfully scraped conversations. Existing model configurations, prompts, and code/data links remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including TopiOCQA, CORAL, WildBench, and conversational-search overviews. Section 4 explicitly positions search-augmented systems as open-web, multi-round RAG, and Appendix G develops comparisons with CORAL and the previously cited WildChat. The main novelty claim is retained.

P1.justification: V2 tightens several paragraphs and captions, expands the validation and limitations discussion, and adds Appendix G while preserving the original section sequence. Author–year citations, revised headings, and conference identification replace the preprint presentation.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figures E.3, G.1, and G.2 and adopts the ICLR template with revised headers, typography, and float placement. Retained displays are largely unchanged apart from renumbering and relocation. A local layout regression makes the Appendix E.3 heading overlap the preceding text on page 34.

improvement.justification: The expert check, additional source and dataset comparisons, and explicit qualifications about subjective preferences and noncausal analysis modestly strengthen evidential support and interpretation. Core results remain unchanged, and the small validation study provides limited assurance. These gains outweigh the localized Appendix E.3 layout defect.
